implementation_notes: The modern Java default is Thymeleaf: a fragment is declared with th:fragment (optionally parameterized, th:fragment="copy(title)") and inserted with th:insert (as the body of the host tag) or th:replace (instead of it) using fragment expressions such as ~{fragments/footer :: copy}, with the engine resolving and rendering it in the calling template's context - the fragment expressions and the template engine are the pattern's View Manager. Fragments evaluate in the caller's context, so pass parameters explicitly; the layout can also be expressed as a th:fragment taking title/content fragments, which replaces tile/JSP layout machinery.
code_sketch: © 2026
pitfalls: th:insert keeps the host element and inserts the fragment as its body while th:replace removes the host tag - confusing them produces duplicated wrappers or missing containers.
Fragments see the calling template's context: a reusable fragment that reads ambient variables breaks on the next page; declare fragment arguments instead.

Fragment expressions are subject to stricter expression restrictions for security reasons, but a fragment name assembled from request data is still an injection/local-file-disclosure risk - allow-list it.

variants.name: JSP static include directive and <jsp:include> action
variants.idiom_name: <%@ include file="..." %> (translation time) and <jsp:include page="..."> (request time)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Java EE form, still specified by Jakarta Pages: <%@ include file="..." %> merges the fragment into the page at translation time (one generated servlet, no per-request cost, but changes require recompilation), while <jsp:include page="..." flush="true"> invokes the target at request time and can pass <jsp:param> values - that is the runtime-inclusion route for fragments whose output depends on the request. Choose these in existing JSP stacks; new applications should use fragment-based engines such as Thymeleaf, which keep the same pattern with safer, more maintainable mechanics.
variants.code_sketch:
<%@ include file="/WEB-INF/jsp/fragments/chrome.jsp" %>  <!-- translation time -->
<c:forEach var="p" items="${products}">
  <jsp:include page="/WEB-INF/jsp/fragments/productRow.jsp"> <!-- request time -->
    <jsp:param name="id" value="${p.id}"/>
  </jsp:include>
</c:forEach>
pitfalls: The static directive merges source before compilation, so the fragment must not declare conflicting page directives (pageEncoding, imports) and any layout change requires recompiling the including pages.
<jsp:include> performs a request dispatch per fragment - use it only for genuinely request-dependent regions, because it dominates rendering cost on fragment-heavy pages.

Variable scope differs: a statically included fragment shares the page's scope, a dynamically included one gets request scope plus explicit <jsp:param> values, so the same fragment can behave differently depending on the inclusion mechanism.
